content: The systematic review included randomized controlled trials conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in Gambia, Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda. One trial assessed the use of monthly sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) until the end of the malaria transmission season. Another trial evaluated monthly artemether-lumefantrine (AL) at four and eight weeks post-discharge. A third trial examined monthly dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-P) at 14, 42, and 70 days post-discharge. The review focused on trials comparing post-discharge malaria chemoprevention (PDMC) with no intervention in children under nine years of age with anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL) or severe anemia (hemoglobin <5 g/dL). The intervention period began with the first dose of the initial PDMC course and continued until four weeks after the first dose of the final course, with a follow-up period of 2–14 weeks. The post-intervention period started the day after the intervention period ended and lasted up to 26 weeks. The AMSTAR-2 checklist determined that the systematic review was of good quality overall. However, five key outcomes—severe malaria, anemia, severe anemia, blood transfusion, and parasite prevalence—were not covered in the review. The Evidence-to-Decision framework summarized the evidence considered by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The GDG concluded that the balance of benefits and harms favored PDMC, with moderate cost savings likely associated with its implementation. PDMC was deemed probably cost-effective, though the certainty of evidence regarding required resources was low. It was also considered likely acceptable to key stakeholders, but the feasibility of large-scale implementation remains uncertain. The GDG recommended a conditional endorsement of PDMC based on moderateto high-certainty evidence of significant beneficial effects and likely low costs. A guide to support PDMC implementation is under development, and a manual for subnational tailoring of malaria interventions is expected to be published in 2023. Written reminders of PDMC treatment dates on children’s health cards were well-received by participants. Most caregivers preferred SMS reminders over community health worker (CHW) visits, though those without phones experienced delays when relying on neighbors or family members for reminders. The GDG noted that the feasibility of PDMC implementation on a broad scale is unclear, given evidence from only three trials, including one implementation study. The optimal approach to PDMC implementation may vary by location and could benefit from direct links between health facilities and community-based care where CHWs are involved. Further information on the evidence is available in the summary of contextual factors report. WHO guidelines recommend routine monitoring of PDMC programs for safety, efficacy, drug resistance, and effectiveness. The impact of PDMC introduction can be evaluated using routine hospital, clinic, or CHW data. The potential effect of PDMC on the spread of drug resistance is likely modest, given the small proportion of the population receiving the intervention. Resistance may be monitored through molecular marker analysis, though the correlation between these markers and antimalarial efficacy for chemoprevention is unclear and should be interpreted cautiously. Additional guidance will be provided in the forthcoming PDMC implementation guide. The GDG identified several evidence gaps requiring further research. For example, mass drug administration (MDA) for malaria involves administering a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medicine to all age groups in a defined geographical area, often at repeated intervals, without prior malaria testing. This approach treats existing infections and prevents new ones during the drug’s prophylactic period. MDA has historically been used to reduce malaria disease burden or transmission. The distinction between these two use cases is somewhat artificial, as interventions that reduce transmission also reduce disease burden and vice versa. The GDG broadly recommended considering MDA to reduce Plasmodium falciparum transmission in very low to low transmission settings and to reduce disease burden in moderate to high transmission settings. A P. falciparum prevalence of around 10% (or an infection incidence of approximately 250 per 1,000 population per year) may differentiate low-to-very-low transmission areas from moderate-to-high transmission areas. These thresholds are not absolute, and MDA near the 10% threshold may reduce both disease burden and transmission intensity. However, the relative effects of burden reduction versus transmission reduction vary along the transmission spectrum. For P. vivax, MDA is more complex due to the potential for relapses unless treated with an 8-aminoquinoline to clear hypnozoites. This drug class can cause severe hemolysis in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, necessitating G6PD testing, pharmacovigilance systems, and emergency access to blood transfusion services. Evidence for MDA’s impact on P. vivax disease reduction was insufficient, though it may contribute to transmission reduction in some settings. A related strategy, mass relapse prevention (MRP), involves administering an 8-aminoquinoline drug to treat hypnozoites and prevent relapses, typically in areas with highly seasonal P. vivax transmission. WHO recommends tailoring intervention packages to local contexts. MDA recommendations are subject to contextual considerations, such as desired impact, endemicity level, and resource availability. Antimalarial medicines used for MDA should differ from first-line malaria treatments and be administered as a directly observed single dose where possible. Limited evidence exists on whether MDA accelerates antimalarial drug resistance development, though available data suggest minimal impact on resistance markers. Contraindications for MDA may include pregnant women in the first trimester, infants under six months or weighing less than 5 kg, individuals recently treated with the same medicine, those with known allergies to the medicine, and individuals with severe acute illness or contraindications to the drug. Information about MDA should be accessible to caregivers, health workers, and stakeholders, with consent obtained before administration.
